body_markdown:
A little while back, I bought a 312,000-mile Toyota Tundra to replace my car commune/shop’s aged and unreliable 1991 Dodge Ram, Fuggles. I blew Fuggles up while smuggling engines back to the shop, and then pawned it off back on the previous owner, Jon, who[found a rebuilt 3.9-liter motor for it](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-moving-shaking-and-spring-cleaning/) . There was, however, still a large tonnage in Fuggles that I needed to remove. So Jon took the 2000 Tundra, which, for the record, I consider a rat-infested pile of high-mileage garbage.


Around, and around, and around, we go.


Loading it up with all the stuff that I’ll fail to take out.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Jon’s reunion didn’t last long, despite the new engine. Maybe something got into him while he was driving a truck that would, I dunno, start every time. He sold Fuggles to some dude in South Carolina who was happy to give him $2200 for it. A few days later, Jon bought an ex-DOT 2013 Silverado.


I am beginning to think that the enjoyment I get from tinkering with trucks is directly at odds with their usefulness. Take the[Roo Chaser](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-l-a-to-detroit-in-the-roo-chaser-part-1/) , for example. The last time I used it for hauling, I blew the transmission up over an expansion joint… at 6000 rpm with 900 pounds of concrete in the back.


All of this navel-gazing has made me eager to report on the Tundra’s doings since it arrived at the Troutman Foundry car collective. It may shock you, dear reader, that it has endured trials and tribulations as our shop truck.


The first item of business when the Tundra arrived was to remove its putrid rodent stench. That proved to be more difficult than expected, so I skipped straight to the second priority: ball joints and control arm bushings. This area is a known weak point for high-mileage Toyota pickups. Anytime you see one stranded on the side of the road with cross-eyed wheels, this is the culprit. Several readers reminded me of this phenomenon in the comments of previous columns, and for that I am grateful, because I would’ve overlooked it otherwise. (And I didn’t want to wear out the new tires…)


Fixing the things y’all told me I had to.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The Tundra’s seller had bragged to me about having put a new set of tires on it not that long ago and, of course, as one often realizes well after purchase, the receipts don’t exactly substantiate the claim. The reality: one set of no-name Chinese tires on the front axle, date-coded 2022, and another, different brand on the rear from 2025. In any case, I didn’t want to prematurely bald them while suffering a ball joint collapse, so I shelled out about $300 on new parts and Thomas, the Foundry’s chief grunt, jammed them in there for me. I splurged on an alignment, too, to fix the cockeyed steering wheel. Now that the truck would traverse down the road on its wonky, loud tires, I could move on to other problems.


The Tundra was leaking an awful lot of oil for being a Toyota. No one had bothered to change the valve cover gaskets yet. It was a good opportunity to go ahead and do plugs as well, but we didn’t quite have the gumption to attack the exhaust leak at the manifold. Good enough!


Next step was trying to achieve a functional milestone: an operational tailgate. As with nearly any 300,000-plus-mile Tundra, the lever had snapped off, requiring an abnormal amount of finesse and usually a pair of pliers. In a primal Foundry firewood-gathering exercise, Thomas felled a large tree on the tailgate, which happily coincided with the arrival of my new handle.


I spent a few minutes with a come-along and eyelet bolt, straightening out the tailgate against the back bed rail and beating along the top bridge of the gate with a hammer and dolly. After getting the piece into as good as it needed to be, I installed the new lever and then promptly sent out an angry group chat message imploring everyone *not* to treat the Tundra like Fuggles.


As time wore on, we treated the truck with respect but did begin to use it in anger, for more serious jobs. Charging and electrical maladies started cropping up. The former we rectified with a new serpentine belt, but occasionally, the truck would fail to start. Late one night, while Thomas was sleeping on the couch at the Foundry, something else entirely took place.


This is what it’s made for.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


According to Thomas’ tale, which security footage backs up, a Buick Enclave pulled into the driveway at three in the morning and started blaring the horn several times, nose to nose with the Tundra. The Buick then promptly left. Thankfully, this was enough to startle Thomas, who ran outside and noticed… the Tundra trying to start itself. The starter was running autonomously for however long its deep-cycle marine battery had lasted to that point. We like self-starters here at the Foundry, but this is the wrong sort.


Not wanting that kind of scare again, or worse yet, an engine bay fire, I splurged on battery cables and a starter relay. The phantom self-starting has yet to happen again, and I began to understand why the previous owner had twice changed the starter. Consider that mystery solved.


OK, now the HVAC upgrades. And by “upgrades,” I mean “weeding through the various smells.” Now well into my Tundra ownership, I was able to discern the various individual odors inside the truck, rather than simply take in the general, foul funk. The rank scent of cigarette smoke dissipated, as did the stale beer and sweat. All that was left was the unmistakable smell of mouse piss.


I first asked Thomas to check the most obvious external locations where a mouse or a rat could gain access. The glove box did contain some chewed-up Taco Bell sauce packets from several years back (lucky vermin: I wish *I* could still get Verde sauce) but no active colonies. With no mice present in the glove box, under the seats, or behind the cowl, it was time to start digging deeper. The first place to check was in the blower assembly, which comes out easily from underneath the dash. It was gross, but there were no mice.


You’re a good man, Thomas.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The damning evidence was the bits of paper towel that came out of the AC vent, indicating that the stinky domicile was located between the evaporator and the vents. Fantastic. I told Thomas to lay waste to the whole assembly, pull the seats, and suck, blast, and wash every bit of mouse nest and urea out of the thing. ( *Editor’s Note* : *When battling mice and their nests, don’t forget to take precautions against hantavirus, which you can[read about here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/hantavirus-may-be-hiding-in-your-classic-heres-how-to-handle-it/)* .)


Later that day, I witnessed Thomas machine-gunning the floors, with the smell of carpet cleaner thick in the air. The truck took several days to dry out, but I will be damned, the mouse smell is gone. Other than the center vents not working and the condensate drain continually washing the passenger side carpet, the issue is rectified.


One more HVAC note: I became quite tired of having to manipulate the temperature knob in the dash with vise grips. Expected a tear-down soon. I ordered a climate control panel, as all the knobs and switches had been filed down to little nubs that looked like canine teeth.


So where does that leave us now? Even with the things I didn’t expect, a $3300 Toyota Tundra is not a bad deal, and even amid the fog of mouse smell it’s been an upgrade over Fuggles. With some elbow grease and maybe another $500 for a windshield and a cut-and-polish, I’ll have something that’s dead reliable, looks decent, and doesn’t smell. Maybe it’s finally time for some name-brand tires?


The post[Against All Oddities: Shop Tundra Saga](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-shop-tundra-saga/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
